newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper fires hawkish armed forces chief.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper fires hawkish armed forces chief.

text.p: The head of Colombia's armed forces, Gen. Harold Bedoya, was fired on Thursday for "reasons of state" in a surprise reshuffle following a series of public disagreements with President Ernesto Samper.

Bedoya, a military hawk, had become increasingly vociferous in his opposition to Samper's plans to launch new peace talks with Colombia's leftist guerrillas. He was replaced by army chief Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett.
There was no immediate word on Bedoya's plans but in an interview last month he said he would consider running for the presidency "if asked" at the conclusion of his military career.
"President Ernesto Samper decided today to introduce changes in the armed forces, taking into account reasons of state," Defence Minister Gilberto Echeverri said in a statement.
"The national government wants to publicly thank Bedoya who fulfilled an important task at the head of the armed forces," he added.

Bedoya, who enjoyed wide support in the ranks and was regarded as a "soldiers' soldier," held the post of armed forces chief for just 8-1/2 months. He was named last October during a bloody guerrilla offensive.
Despite his counterinsurgency experience and training at the U.S. School of the Americas, Bedoya failed to stem the mushrooming rebel onslaught.

Bedoya, whom human rights groups accused of backing right- wing death squads, consistently called for a stronger hand against the country's estimated 18,000 rebels, demanding more equipment and troops. Government ministers called instead for greater efficiency in military spending.

The military chief warned in June that Samper's proposed peace talks would allow the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Latin America's oldest and largest rebel army, to ram the "law of the jungle, the law of the strongest and most violent" down Colombia's throat.

Samper's decision to fire Bedoya comes less than a week after he firmed up his proposals to launch a state-sponsored peace process. Echeverri is due to submit a bill to Congress that will pave the way for the creation of a National Peace Council, made up of political, labour and social representatives, later this week.

In recent months graffiti has been scrawled on walls around Bogota saying: "Bedoya for president." In a radio interview in June, the outgoing armed forces chief described it as a "spontaneous" show of support for somebody who is "not prepared to hand over the country to terrorists."

He said then he would consider running for the presidency. Unlike civilian candidates for the 1998 presidential elections, there is no deadline by which retiring members of the military have to declare their candidacy.

Bedoya has close ties with political hardliners in the opposition Conservative Party and the ruling Liberal Party. Colombia's last military ruler was Gen. Gustavo Rojas Pinilla, who seized power in 1953 amid a 10-year civil war.

The new armed forces chief, Gen. Bonett, was like Bedoya trained at the School of the Americas and has been accused of human rights violations by international and domestic organisations. Political analyst Eduardo Pizarro, however, said he was "more flexible" than Bedoya.
